articles.title: Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?
articles.summary: The real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements

blocks.text: PART 1 | Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach usPART 2 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?

The Ambani brothers got what they wanted in 2005: the freedom to run their businesses without having to answer to each other. Their mother, Kokilaben, helped divide the Reliance empire founded by their father, Dhirubhai Ambani. Mukesh, the elder brother, took control of the oil, petrochemicals, and refining businesses. Anil, the younger, received interests in telecommunications, power, and financial services.

More than two decades later, the brothers’ business fortunes could hardly be more different. Mukesh built Reliance Industries into one of India’s largest companies, expanding into telecommunications through Jio and consumer businesses through Reliance Retail. Anil’s business empire, once valued in the billions of dollars, suffered heavy debts, corporate insolvencies, and the collapse of some of its most prominent enterprises. Both brothers gained independence, but only one turned that freedom into a sustained expansion.

That 20-year history offers a sobering preview for Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, Federico “Piki” Lopez, and the other third generation heirs now unbundling their own family family empire in the Philippines. Following Gabby’s P11.56-billion exit from Lopez Inc. in August, Piki’s September board consolidation at Lopez Holdings and FPH, and FPH’s November approval to sell Rockwell Land to Gabby’s Crème Investment Corp. for almost P16 billion, the Lopezes are moving toward separate corporate spheres. (Click these links below for the author’s special reports on these developments:
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

The cousins are not dividing their group in the exact same way the Ambanis did, nor is their separation complete. Yet the questions hanging over both families are remarkably similar: Will the businesses become stronger when the relatives no longer have to agree on how they should be run? Will the separation end the fighting? And what happens to the shareholders, employees, and younger heirs who must live with the consequences?
The real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

The first two installments of this series examined why business families fight, whether they should stay together or separate, and how they can negotiate a division of their interests. This final installment looks at what happened to families that went through the process years earlier.
After all, the real test of a family divorce begins after the relatives sign their agreements.

The Ambanis offer one of the clearest long-term tests of a family-business separation because enough time has passed to examine what each brother did with the businesses he controlled. In the financial year ending March 2026, Reliance Industries reported consolidated revenue of ₹11.76 trillion and profit after tax of about ₹95,754 crore. Its telecommunications business served more than 524 million subscribers, while its retail operations had grown to more than 20,000 stores. Mukesh had not merely preserved the oil and petrochemicals businesses he inherited, he had used their financial strength to build major new businesses in industries that barely figured in the family’s original empire.

Anil’s experience was very different. Reliance Communications, once a major competitor in India’s telecommunications industry, entered insolvency proceedings after accumulating debts it could not service. The company became subject to a court-supervised resolution process, and Anil resigned from its board in 2019. Other businesses associated with his group also underwent financial difficulties and restructuring. The Reliance Group even emphasized that Reliance Communications is no longer under Anil’s management and that its remaining operating companies should be assessed separately.

It would be convenient to conclude that Mukesh made the right choices and Anil made the wrong ones. But that would oversimplify what happened. Telecommunications changed dramatically as competition intensified, particularly after Mukesh’s Jio entered the market in 2016. Financing decisions, accumulated debt, industry regulation, and the timing of investments all influenced the brothers’ fortunes. The 2005 division gave them freedom to make those decisions. It did not determine how those decisions would turn out.

There is also another question: Did the separation actually end their disputes? Not entirely. The brothers subsequently fought over the supply and pricing of natural gas, a disagreement that reached India’s Supreme Court. Their businesses were separate, but they still had commercial interests that brought them into conflict. Later reports of Mukesh helping Anil meet a financial obligation suggested that the relationship was more complicated than an unbroken feud, although such episodes cannot establish the state of their private relationship.

The Ambanis’ experience illustrates the difference between settling a family dispute and succeeding in business afterward. The brothers gained control of their respective enterprises. What they accomplished with that control was another matter.

The Bajaj family’s experience reinforces the point. The division of its business interests gave different branches greater independence, but the companies that emerged from the arrangement did not enjoy identical fortunes.

Bajaj Auto has become one of India’s major motorcycle and three-wheeler manufacturers. In the financial year ending March 2026, it reported record standalone revenue of ₹58,732 crore and profit after tax of ₹9,825 crore, an increase of more than 20% from the previous year. The wider Bajaj financial-services businesses have also expanded significantly. Bajaj Finance reported assets under management exceeding ₹5 trillion in the same financial year.

Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar, associated with Shishir Bajaj’s branch, experienced a more difficult period. Its 2026 annual report described financial pressures arising from high sugarcane procurement costs, relatively flat sugar prices, and difficulties servicing debt. The company reported a loss of ₹751 crore for the previous financial year before returning to a reported profit of about ₹138 crore in the year ending March 2026. Its November 2026 financial disclosures continued to discuss restructuring arrangements and the need to manage liquidity.

The difference is striking, but it is not proof that the Bajaj separation benefited one branch at the expense of another. Motorcycles, financial services, and sugar are very different businesses. They face different markets, regulatory requirements, and operating risks. Sugar producers in India, for example, are affected by government policies governing cane prices and sugar sales, factors that have little to do with disagreements among shareholders.

What the Bajaj experience does demonstrate is that once relatives gain control of their respective businesses, their fortunes increasingly depend on the companies they manage and the industries in which they operate.
The separation may have settled who controlled the businesses, but it did not guarantee how those businesses would perform.
Not every family dispute ends with relatives dividing an entire conglomerate. Sometimes independence means leaving the management of a business while building another enterprise.

Walter Kwok, the eldest of three brothers who inherited Hong Kong property developer Sun Hung Kai Properties, lost his leadership position following a prolonged dispute with his brothers. He subsequently established Empire Group Holdings, pursuing property development outside the company his father had founded.

Walter died in 2018, but Empire continued operating. The privately held company has undertaken residential, commercial, and hospitality developments, demonstrating that Walter established a substantial business outside Sun Hung Kai. That does not establish whether he became wealthier than he would have been had he remained in charge of the family company.

But his experience illustrates something important about family-business disputes: ownership, management, and independence are not necessarily the same thing. A family member may lose the right to run a company without losing all financial interests in it. Another may choose to surrender a position in an established enterprise to pursue opportunities elsewhere.
The question is not always who gets to keep the family company. It can also be whether the relatives are better able to pursue their ambitions without constantly contesting control.
There is another measure of success that cannot be found in a company’s financial statements: whether the relatives themselves are able to move beyond the conflict.

The Ambani brothers’ dispute over natural gas showed that dividing ownership does not necessarily eliminate commercial disagreements. Even after companies have been separated, relatives may remain connected through contracts, investments, obligations, and the history of decisions made when the businesses were still together.

Other family disputes have demonstrated how difficult it can be to separate corporate disagreements from personal relationships. In the Philippines, the Ilusorio family’s conflict extended into disputes over family authority and the care of elderly parents. The Yanson family’s disagreement over the Vallacar Transit group involved competing claims to management and ownership that produced years of legal proceedings. Those histories were discussed in Part 1 and 2 of this series.

But a separation need not restore close personal relationships to succeed as a business arrangement. Relatives who can no longer work together may prefer to run their businesses independently and maintain a more distant personal relationship. That may be preferable than remaining partners in an enterprise where every major decision becomes another family confrontation.
Corporate peace, however, should not be confused with family peace.

The distinction becomes especially important when the relatives belong to a family whose businesses have been associated with its identity for generations. Disagreements over corporate control can become disagreements over legacy: who deserves to lead, whose contribution matters most, and who has the right to decide what happens to the assets accumulated by parents and grandparents.
A separation may reduce the occasions for corporate disagreement. Whether it changes the relationships among relatives is a different question.
A family settlement can be satisfactory to the relatives who negotiated it and still create problems for their children.

The Ambani family’s experience offers an opportunity to examine the next stage. Mukesh’s children—Isha, Akash, and Anant—have assumed increasingly prominent responsibilities in the Reliance businesses. Akash chairs Reliance Jio Infocomm, Isha has played a leading role in retail, and Anant has taken on responsibilities in the group’s energy and other businesses. The family’s succession arrangements are being developed within the enterprise Mukesh expanded after the 2005 separation.

That development is significant because the original division did more than establish which brother controlled which assets. It created separate business structures within which their descendants would eventually exercise ownership and management responsibilities.

The Bajaj family offers another example of business interests passing to younger generations after an earlier division. But a clear separation among branches does not automatically resolve every future succession question. Children and grandchildren may eventually disagree among themselves over who should manage a company, how profits should be distributed, or whether particular assets should be sold.

Family-business advisers Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer have written about how family feuds can threaten businesses when money, authority, and personal relationships become intertwined. Their work is a useful reminder that removing one source of conflict does not necessarily eliminate the conditions that produced it.

Asian family business adviser Enrique Soriano makes a related point about inheritance: He argued that passing ownership to the next generation does not necessarily mean passing on a business capable of functioning successfully under its new owners. Inheriting shares and being equipped to manage a company are different matters. His point raises another way of judging family settlements: Should success be measured by what the relatives accomplish immediately after separating, or by what happens when their children and grandchildren take over? (READ: If great business dynasties can fracture, why would your family be any different?)

For the Lopezes, that question may be answered only 10 or 20 years from now. Their younger heirs will inherit not only the businesses that Gabby, Piki, and their third generation cousins choose to retain, but also the ownership arrangements, financial obligations, and family relationships left by the current dispute. Whether those arrangements prove durable may ultimately be a more meaningful measure of success than the agreements reached today.
The longer-term test of a family settlement may therefore come when the next generation begins exercising the ownership and leadership rights established by their parents.

When business families fight, the headlines usually focus on the relatives: who controls the company, who gets the assets, and how much each branch receives. But the consequences extend to people who did not participate in the dispute and have little influence over its outcome.

Reliance Communications’ insolvency left creditors dealing with a court-supervised resolution process. Bajaj Hindusthan Sugar’s financial difficulties required negotiations with lenders over debt and liquidity. Neither company’s difficulties can simply be blamed on its family’s earlier separation. They nevertheless demonstrate that the financial decisions of controlling shareholders and managers can have consequences far beyond their own fortunes.

For the Lopez group, the changes have also been felt in its boardrooms and executive offices. Long-serving executives have left positions they held for years, while changes in shareholdings have brought new directors and altered the composition of boards. One significant departure was Salvador Tirona. He had worked with the Lopezes since early 2000s-and served as president, chief operating officer, and chief finance officer of Lopez Holdings. At the September 14 annual meeting, Piki’s brother Jay Lopez took over Tirona’s executive positions. Tirona also resigned from ABS-CBN Holdings, where he had served as chairman and held senior executive posts.

Another longtime corporate officer, Enrique Quiason, resigned as corporate secretary of First Philippine Holdings in November after nearly 34 years with the company. Both Tirona and Quiason resigned—not retired—during a period of major changes in ownership and leadership, although neither cited the family feud as the reason for leaving.

Earlier, when the cousins were exchanging increasingly hostile public statements, two independent directors of Lopez Holdings also stepped down. Roberto Panlilio resigned effective May 1, followed by Consuelo Garcia on May 5. Both cited personal reasons. Their departures left the seven-member board with only one independent director at the time.

The family conflict was also being discussed directly with employees. At a First Gen town hall on April 17, Piki acknowledged the dispute but urged employees not to become involved in choosing between the warring relatives. “There’s no need for you to take sides,” he said. He described the fight as a shareholder conflict that would eventually work itself out. His message was to remain professional and continue doing their jobs.

At ABS-CBN, employees received a more difficult message. During a September 15 town hall, president and CEO Carlo Katigbak announced another round of retrenchments—around 200 employees, or 7% of its workforce—even as the company was preparing to receive P6 billion in fresh capital from the Lopez family and other investors. Katigbak told employees that this would be the last retrenchment program under his leadership, but it followed years of job cuts since ABS-CBN lost its broadcast franchise in 2020, when about 5,000 employees were retrenched.

blocks.caption: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way

blocks.text: The contrast between the new investments and the latest job losses was difficult to ignore. The additional capital was intended to help ABS-CBN recover, but it did not remove the need to reduce expenses. In its September statement, the company cited weak advertising and consumer spending, inflation, and difficult conditions in the content industry.

The retrenchments cannot be solely attributed to the bitter Lopez family feud. ABS-CBN’s financial difficulties began years before the cousins’ dispute became public. But the layoffs demonstrate why the outcome of the family’s business decisions matters to people outside the family. For employees, a successful turnaround is not simply a stronger balance sheet or the arrival of new investors. It is a company capable of sustaining jobs and paying the people who work for it. (READ: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?)

Creditors have their own concerns. ABS-CBN must demonstrate that it can generate enough cash to meet its obligations, including loans that may require refinancing or extensions. Banks will have to assess whether the company’s recovery plans provide a credible basis for continued lending.

Minority shareholders also have a stake in what happens next. Rockwell’s public shareholders face a proposed change in control. FPH’s November disclosure states that the transaction requires, among other conditions, a mandatory tender offer by Crème to other Rockwell shareholders. The terms of that offer will matter to investors who did not participate in the family’s negotiations.

For employees, the test is whether the businesses can sustain jobs. For creditors, it is whether debts are repaid. For minority shareholders, it is whether their investments are protected and rewarded.
These interests do not always coincide with those of the relatives negotiating a settlement. They cannot be left out when judging whether a corporate divorce worked.

The experiences of the Ambanis and Bajajs bring us back to the Lopezes. Their separations gave different family branches the freedom to pursue their own business strategies. But the results depended on what businesses they controlled, the investments they made, the risks they took, and their ability to finance those decisions.

For Federico “Piki” Lopez, the future increasingly depends on energy. His group is committing enormous resources to renewable power and infrastructure projects that may take years to complete and even longer to recover their investment costs.

Geothermal energy, pumped-storage hydropower, and other large projects require substantial capital upfront. They involve technical studies, regulatory approvals, financing, construction, and agreements for selling the electricity they will eventually produce. Delays can increase costs, while changes in electricity prices and financing conditions can affect returns.

The Lopez group has decades of experience in the power business. But experience does not remove the risks of committing large amounts of capital to projects whose expected earnings lie years, if not decades, ahead.

The question is whether Piki is making the right investments now to secure substantial earnings years from today. Will the projects produce enough cash to justify their cost? Can the group finance the years of development without taking on excessive debt? And will selling Rockwell, an established property business, prove a worthwhile exchange for the capital needed to pursue those ambitions?

FPH has told the stock exchange that selling Rockwell would allow it to redirect resources toward energy, infrastructure, and other businesses where it sees opportunities. The proposed transaction would bring in nearly P16 billion, but the amount of cash raised is only one measure of its value. The more important test is what FPH eventually earns from the investments it makes with that money.

blocks.caption: The company the Lopezes gave up Meralco for: EDC, from oil crisis child to takeover target

blocks.text: For Gabby Lopez and the majority cousins, the challenge is almost the opposite. They are committing resources to ABS-CBN at a time when the economics of the media industry are being rewritten.

Before losing its franchise, ABS-CBN produced television programs and distributed them through its own nationwide broadcast network. It controlled much of the process, from creating shows to delivering them to viewers and selling advertising around those audiences. Today, ABS-CBN remains a content producer but relies on broadcast partners, streaming services, and digital platforms to reach audiences. It must negotiate distribution arrangements, compete for attention across multiple platforms, and find ways to earn enough from its content in a market where viewers and advertisers have more choices. (READ: Streaming services ‘winning hearts and minds’ of Filipinos, says new study)

The P6-billion capital infusion may provide breathing room, but it cannot by itself establish a profitable business model. Can ABS-CBN consistently earn more from its content than it spends producing and distributing it? Can it control costs without sacrificing the talent and production capabilities that remain its principal strengths? And can it generate sufficient cash to meet its obligations rather than depend on repeated financial support?

blocks.caption: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red

blocks.text: The proposed acquisition of Rockwell adds another dimension to Gabby’s bet. Rockwell has established assets and earnings, but acquiring it requires substantial capital. Its cash flows must first support its own operations, development projects, financing requirements, and shareholders. How much, if anything, could eventually be available to support the other investments of Gabby’s branch?

Nor should Rockwell’s profits automatically be treated as money available to ABS-CBN. The two companies have different shareholders, creditors, and financial obligations. Rockwell’s ability to distribute cash to its owners depends on its own financial condition and corporate requirements. Whether Gabby’s branch can use such distributions to support ABS-CBN will also depend on how the Rockwell acquisition is financed and which entities receive the dividends.
That brings both sides to a question that rarely features prominently in accounts of family feuds: Will their bankers continue to have confidence in them?

Piki’s group must finance projects whose expected returns lie years ahead. Gabby’s branch must manage the cost of a major acquisition while supporting a media business still searching for sustainable profitability.

For ABS-CBN, the debt question is particularly pressing. Its ability to meet repayment schedules, refinance obligations, and retain access to bank credit will depend partly on whether its operating performance improves.

Extending loan maturities can be a normal part of corporate financing. But when a business repeatedly needs more time because it cannot generate enough cash to meet its obligations, lenders must reassess the risks.

The relevant questions are not simply how much debt ABS-CBN owes, but when its loans fall due, how much interest it must pay, whether its operations generate enough cash, and what security or guarantees its lenders hold. Those obligations must also be distinguished from any financing arrangements used by Crème or other companies to acquire Rockwell.

Banks have their own reasons for supporting companies through difficult periods. They may prefer a workable restructuring to an immediate default. But their willingness to extend credit is not unlimited. A turnaround must eventually demonstrate that the borrower can repay what it owes.
The separation may give each cousin greater control over the businesses he believes in. It also makes the consequences of those choices more clearly his responsibility.
The Lopezes may eventually discover what the Ambanis learned after their own division: freedom to pursue a business strategy and success in carrying it out are two very different things.

blocks.caption: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The experiences of other families offer no guarantee that the Lopez separation will work. The Ambanis demonstrate that independence can produce dramatically different business fortunes. The Bajajs show that the industries and financial circumstances inherited by each branch matter enormously. Walter Kwok’s experience shows that leaving an established family enterprise need not mean the end of a business career.

None of these examples proves that separation is always preferable to remaining together. They demonstrate that settling ownership is one achievement. Making the resulting businesses successful is another.

For the Lopezes, the immediate questions concern whether the proposed transactions are completed and whether the new ownership arrangements establish more stable control. But the harder questions will take much longer to answer.

Will Piki’s large investments in energy generate the returns needed to justify their cost? Can Gabby’s branch build a sustainable future for ABS-CBN in an industry whose business model is still changing? Will Rockwell prove a valuable investment without becoming an excessive financial burden? And can both sides generate enough cash to repay creditors, finance their ambitions, and reward shareholders?
And when the next generation takes over, will it inherit companies capable of prospering under the arrangements made today—or another set of disputes over ownership and control?

A family settlement can end the argument over who owns what and who gets to run the business. It cannot guarantee that the companies will prosper, that the relatives will reconcile, or that their children will be spared another fight.

For the Lopezes, the separation may finally give each branch greater freedom to pursue its own ambitions. Whether that freedom produces stronger businesses, healthier relationships, and a better future for the next generation will take years to discover. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Teenager allegedly organised arsons and kidnapping on Signal during Melbourne hospitality wars
articles.summary:
Victoria police say boy, 17, communicated with offenders under username ‘Onepercent’

  • Get our breaking news…

blocks.text: Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.
The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.
He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.

In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.
The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.
It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.

Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.
It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.
On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.
“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.
“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.
“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

articles.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles.summary: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
articles.byline: Shaimaa Khalil, Harry Sekulich, Chris Graham

blocks.text: Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and United States President Donald Trump, arrived in Manila for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

On November 14, regional leaders signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA), the first region-wide agreement of its kind. The milestone established common rules for digital trade and payments. The bloc also advanced initiatives on maritime cooperation, disaster response, online scams, and child protection.
The 49th ASEAN Summit resulted in over a hundred outcome documents but failed to resolve ongoing issues such as the civil war in Myanmar and the South China Sea Code of Conduct negotiations.

“I would say that it was a success simply because of the work that we were able to achieve. The one thing I did not want to do was to waste an opportunity such as this by just doing this hosting,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. told the media following the summit’s closing ceremony on November 17.

Meanwhile, activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump’s visit gathered on November 15 to protest. Police blocked their march resulting in skirmishes and arrests. Nearly 300 were detained in Manila and Las Pinas City. On November 18, the demonstrators were released due to lack of evidence.

articles.title: 'He's a killer': Zelensky reacts to Trump calling Putin a friend
articles.summary: Trump's comments came as Russia launched "biggest attacks this year" against Ukraine.

blocks.text: Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

articles.title: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
articles.summary:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the…

blocks.text: Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

blocks.caption: Aerial view of a burnt Rohingya village near Maungdaw in Myanmar in September 2017.  Photograph: Soe Zeya Tun/Reuters

blocks.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.
For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.
Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.
Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees in Kutapalong camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, in 2017.  Photograph: Allison Joyce/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.
Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.
Momtaz and Dildar Begum

blocks.caption: Sisters Dildar Begum (left) and Momtaz Begum. Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian

blocks.text: Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.
It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.
In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.
Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.
Anwara Begum

blocks.caption: Anwara Begum in the Cox’s Bazar refugee camp, Bangladesh. Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian

blocks.text: Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.
When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.
She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.
Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.
To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.
Nur Alam

blocks.caption: Nur Alam has been a refugee in Bangladesh four times over his life. Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian

blocks.text: Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.
His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

articles.title: OVP: Tree planting campaign not associated with Cale88 BOI compliance
articles.summary: The Office of the Vice President (OVP) on Saturday denied that its "Pagbabago: A Million Trees Campaign" is related to Cale88 Foods Corporation's compliance with the Board of Investments' (BOI)…

blocks.text: Published November 21, 2026 11:25am

The Office of the Vice President (OVP) on Saturday denied that its "Pagbabago: A Million Trees Campaign" is related to Cale88 Foods Corporation's compliance with the Board of Investments' (BOI) tree-planting requirement.
This comes a day after the House prosecution panel raised questions about the activity during the impeachment trial on Friday.

"The Office of the Vice President (OVP) categorically denies any association between its "Pagbabago: A Million Trees Campaign" and Cale88 Foods Corporation's compliance with the Board of Investments' (BOI) tree-planting requirement," the OVP said in a statement.

"Any attempt to link the Vice President's participation in the OVP's environmental initiatives to Cale88 Foods Corporation's BOI compliance is misleading, malicious, and has no factual basis," it added.

Cale88, the food firm linked to Duterte's husband Manases Carpio, has come under scrutiny during the impeachment trial over its profits earned with only two employees and its supposed financial inflows from China.
During the cross examination of Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo on Day 45 of the trial, private prosecutor Erwin Matib flashed photos of Duterte planting trees.
"Tama po ba na itong pagtatanim ng mga puno ni Vice President Sara Duterte ay connected sa pag-comply ng Cale88 Foods sa tree planting activities na requirement ng Board of Investment?" Matib asked.
(Is it correct that Vice President Sara Duterte tree planting is connected with with Cale88's compliance with the tree planting requirements of the Board of Investment?)
Before Rodolfo could answer, defense counsel Justin Gular objected.

"Objection, your honor, misleading. There is no prior testimony coming from the witness wherein he testified that the vice president participated in the compliance requirement of tree planting," Gullar said.
Presiding Officer Francis Escudero sustained Gular's objection, telling Matib to carry on to the next point.
The OVP, meanwhile, said that its tree planting campaign is an "independent environmental initiative."

"The "Pagbabago: A Million Trees Campaign" is an independent environmental initiative of the OVP, launched on March 27, 2023, in support of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources' (DENR) efforts to reduce carbon emissions and address climate change," it said.

"The program is part of the OVP's advocacy to protect the environment for future generations. To date, the campaign, in partnership with various government agencies and private sectors, has planted 1,386,682 trees nationwide," added the OVP. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Brazil ex-president Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
articles.summary: Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.

image.caption: Bolsonaro ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections (FILE: September 14, 2025)Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP

blocks.text: Convicted former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.
Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."
The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.
Bolsonaro's history of hospitalizations
​Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.
"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.
Son blames house arrest for Bolsonaro's health issues

Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to ​2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.
Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.
Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.
Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."
Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

articles.title: UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
articles.summary: Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions…

image.caption: Daniel Thomas, also known as "Danny Tommo," founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform [FILE: July 31, 2024]Image: Benjamin Cremel/AFP

blocks.text: A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.
Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.

blocks.caption: British anti-migrant activist Danny Tommo was sentenced to 15 months in prison at Portsmouth Crown Court [FILE: September 29, 2026]Image: Justin Tallis/AFP

blocks.text: The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.
What happened during the English Channel incident?
Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.
After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.
Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.

blocks.caption: Migrants are rescued from the sea after a failed attempt to board a small boat to cross the English Channel to the UK near Dunkirk, northern France [FILE: July 30, 2026]Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."
He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.
Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.
What did the judge say about Danny Tommo's actions?
Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.
The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).
"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.

blocks.caption: Migrants rescued at sea by the UK's Border Force disembark from a patrol vessel in Dover after attempting to cross the English Channel from France [FILE: May 21, 2025]Image: Ben Stansall/AFP

blocks.text: Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.
He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.
Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.
The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.
Who is Danny Tommo and what is Patriot Platform?
Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.
He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.

blocks.caption: Far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London facing charges of harassing two journalists [FILE: October 10, 2026]Image: Jordan Pettitt/Press Association/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.
The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.
The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."
Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.
Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

articles.title: ‘A new imperial age’: Yuval Harari warns Philippines of foreign AI dependence
articles.summary: The best-selling author of 'Sapiens' and 'Nexus' warns that AI could usher in a new age of empires and leave countries like the Philippines dependent on foreign powers

blocks.text: FUTURE. Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and historian Yuval Noah Harari talk about the future of AI for humanity.
Rappler
The best-selling author of 'Sapiens' and 'Nexus' warns that AI could usher in a new age of empires and leave countries like the Philippines dependent on foreign powers

items: Historian Yuval Noah Harari warns that countries like the Philippines risk losing control over critical infrastructure due to dependence on foreign AI technologies from superpowers like the US and China.

Harari suggests that the Philippines should consider cooperating with regional partners such as Japan and Australia to develop shared AI capabilities instead of solely relying on foreign systems or building independent infrastructure.
He emphasizes the importance of political intervention in AI development, advocating for a focus on safety and practical applications rather than a race toward superintelligence.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – As the Philippines finds its place in the global artificial intelligence (AI) industry, historian and best-selling author Yuval Noah Harari warned that countries outside the world’s leading technology powers risk losing control of critical infrastructure unless they develop their own capabilities or cooperate with regional partners.

Speaking with Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa at a pre-recorded conversation for the 2026 Social Good Summit, Harari said the concentration of AI technology in superpowers like the United States and China could usher in a new era of economic and political dependence.
“We are entering a new imperial age,” Harari said. “The empires are back.”

And this time, he warned, could be even worse. Consider how the Romans and the British – powerful as their empires were – remained constrained by geography and physical resources. But now with AI, control of its infrastructure and frontier models could concentrate economic and military power in ways previously impossible.
As lesser powers become dependent on foreign AI systems to run hospitals, airports, and military equipment, that could raise their vulnerability to decisions made abroad.
“In that situation, you’re no longer independent, you are a vassal state,” Harari said.
For the Philippines, which Ressa described as having been a testing ground for social media platforms, the concern revives many old fears.
“We were the petri dish for social media,” Ressa said, recalling how Facebook became a breeding ground for disinformation and political manipulation during Rodrigo Duterte’s rise to power in 2016.
Could the specter of what Harari calls “data colonialism” be coming back to haunt the Philippines, this time through its ambitions under Pax Silica?

The US-led initiative promises to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing, and AI technologies. After joining the initiative in April 2026, the Philippines unveiled plans for a roughly 1,600-hectare advanced manufacturing hub in New Clark City, Tarlac. As of November, Manila and Washington were still working toward a framework agreement. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has sought to allay concerns by saying no data centers would be built in the area.

But beyond concerns over its energy and water use is another question often missing from discussions on Pax Silica. Would joining global AI supply chains give the Philippines greater control over the technology, or merely a role in manufacturing it?

For Harari, countries outside the US and China face three choices. They could remain dependent on foreign AI infrastructure, spend enormous sums building their own, or pool resources with other countries to develop shared capabilities.

He suggested the last option for the Philippines—working alongside partners such as Japan and Australia. Such cooperation could be cheaper than developing independent infrastructure, but would require closer political coordination.
Harari rejected the argument that AI development was already beyond political intervention.
“What the companies are now trying to do is to convince us that it’s too late to do politics,” he said. “It’s not yet deterministic, it’s not inevitable, there are still choices to be made.”

AI, Harari said, is particularly dangerous because an agent is capable of making decisions, rather than being just a tool fully controlled by humans. And that leash used to keep autonomous AI under human control has already begun to slip.

In July 2026, agents powered by OpenAI models broke out of a restricted test environment and accessed live systems at AI platform Hugging Face, apparently seeking answers to a cybersecurity evaluation.

Anthropic, the company behind Claude, also reported that its models had gone rouge and hacked computer systems of other organizations. Months later, that same company went on to raise $81 billion in the world’s largest IPO in November, beating the record that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had set just months earlier.

In light of all this, Harari argued that governments need not halt AI development outright, but should reconsider the race toward superintelligence and invest more in safety. He urged greater focus on practical uses in healthcare, education, transportation, and public services.
“A product which is not safe is just not useful,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DOTr eyes barrier-less tollways pilot testing before end of 2026
articles.summary: The Department of Transportation is eyeing to implement a barrier-less tollways system across all toll roads before the end of the year.

blocks.text: Published November 21, 2026 9:33am
The Department of Transportation (DOTr) is eyeing to implement a barrier-less tollways system across all toll roads before the end of the year.

In an order, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon said the plan is “in line with our shared commitment to modernizing our road networks, eliminating bottlenecks at toll plazas, and delivering a seamless, world-class travel experience for the motoring public.”
With this, Dizon said that the full implementation of a “Barrier-less/Multi-Lane Free Flow (MFF) Program” across all expressways has become an “urgent national priority.”
“To achieve these benefits, we are targeting the pilot test/proof of concept of the MLFF Program across all expressways before the end of this year,” the Transportation chief said.
Dizon further said that the success of a barrier-less system relies heavily on “near-universal” adoption of cashless payments and “robust backend infrastructure.”
Thus, the DOTr ordered toll roads operators to submit a comprehensive “Action Plan and Readiness Assessment” for the expressways under their jurisdiction.
The following key components should be included in the submission:

• Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Penetration Strategies: Concrete, time-bound initiatives to aggressively increase RFID/ETC adoption among motorists (e.g., expanded installation sites, digital onboarding, promotional incentives, and public information campaigns)

• Infrastructure and Technology Readiness: Current status and deployment timelines for gantries, Automatic Number/License Plate Recognition (ALPR/ANPR) cameras, high-speed RFID readers, and system integration
• Operational and Enforcement Protocols: Proposed mechanisms for handling non-registered vehicles, insufficient balances, and interoperability across different expressway operators
• Implementation Timeline and Milestones: A month-by-month roadmap detailing testing phases, dry ruins, and target dates for full live operation.

“Given the tight timeline and the immediate need to alleviate traffic congestion for our commuters, kindly submit your comprehensive report to this office on or before 21 December 2026 through the Toll Regulatory Board,” Dizon said.
The Transportation chief said that transitioning to a barrier-less system is “no longer merely an operational upgrade; it is an economic necessity.”

“By removing physical toll barriers, we can significantly reduce travel time, lower fuel consumption and carbon emissions caused by idling vehicles, and maximize the overall throughput and efficiency of our expressway infrastructure,” he said. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
articles.summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.

blocks.text: Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

articles.title: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
articles.summary: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.

blocks.text: Image source, Gallo Images via Getty Images
The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021

The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

blocks.caption: Image caption, ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities

blocks.text: ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?

It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.
"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.
Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".
