articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
articles.summary:
Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen

An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on…

blocks.text: An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York ⁠City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the ​235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal ‌court.
The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear ​whether he has hired a defense lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”
Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta said ​he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

articles.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
articles.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.

blocks.text: A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."
Nadine Yousif contributed to this report.

articles.title: Better educated than ever – yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future
articles.summary: Never before have young people faced so many challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off later in life than my parents are now?

image.caption: GenZ makes its voices heard, also on the streets of BerlinImage: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP

blocks.text: It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing professional training or university. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city and finally starting to live independently is nearly impossible.

Nor do young people feel that politicians are finally taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It therefore shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe are taking to the streets this Friday to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 cities, coinciding with World Children's Day.

What particularly infuriates young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example from the political realm was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran the headline: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests," he argues.

blocks.caption: Erik Sczygiol was deputy secretary-general of the German Conference of Student Representatives until recentlyImage: Oliver Pieper/DW

blocks.text: Gen Z is better educated but faces a bleaker future

However, eighteen-year-old Erik Sczygiol is an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW).This year's report is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z. The report is titled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future."

The United Nations surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries. Some of the findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them. Today, 78% of adolescents complete at least upper-secondary education. Yet finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise across the globe.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, financial independence is often not achieved until one's mid-to-late twenties, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities until one's early-to-mid thirties.
Young people are underrepresented in the German parliament

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

At least Brod is somewhat closer to the political decision-making process. He has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

blocks.caption: Florian Brod has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two yearsImage: Oliver Pieper/DW

blocks.text: Political participation often remains purely symbolic

Nevertheless, both Florian Brod and Erik Sczygiol, who represents students, have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."
'Small extremist minority' turn Germany's youth protests violent
The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true

Medical student Amélie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva this May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said, 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We, young people, need to be able to believe in our future again!"

articles.title: Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster opening
articles.summary: Other tech companies have also taken a hit as share markets broadly slump.

blocks.text: Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte camp asks ICC to reject ex-Davao City cop's prior recorded testimony
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - For former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team, the testimony of the ex-Davao City police officer sought by International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors to be admitted…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czech Republic – For former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team, the testimony of the ex-Davao City police officer sought by International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors to be admitted in court has “serious deficiencies” and must be rejected by Trial Chamber III.

Duterte’s counsel Peter Haynes contests the admission of P-0002’s evidence, saying the articles invoked by the Office of the Prosecutor to collect and preserve it require proof that a witness can no longer testify orally.
“Absent such proof, the prior recorded testimony cannot be admitted and the witness must be called to give his evidence viva voce,” Haynes said in a public redacted filing released on November 18.

Haynes’ legal challenge comes roughly ten days before the ICC’s trial of the former president opens, with information still unclear about which witness testimony and evidence will be admitted in court.
Haynes described P-0002 as a “central Prosecution witness” and said his testimony is the most heavily cited in the prosecution’s trial brief.

Prosecutors seek to admit P-0002’s preserved testimony under Article 69(4), following what they described as a “unique opportunity” to interview him and obtain evidence that “may not be subsequently available.”

The prosecution also informed the chamber that P-0002 is “no longer available” to testify before the court. The filing conceals the details of that significant risk, as well as the reason for P-0002’s expected absence.

The Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) support the admission of P-0002’s evidence, which they described as having “particular importance” due to his “position and first-hand knowledge”, which makes his testimony “particularly significant” in the former president’s case.
Defense, prosecution clash over evidence
Duterte’s lawyers dispute how the prosecution obtained P-0002’s evidence, questioning whether it has adequately established its unavailability.
Aside from arguing that the prosecution has no documentary evidence to support P-0002’s evidence, Haynes also questioned the reliability of the former policeman’s account.

He pointed to alleged inconsistencies concerning charged Incident 1, including differences over the year of the incident, the number of victims, the perpetrators, and the circumstances of the killings.

In the Prosecution’s Trial Brief, Incident 1 refers to the killing of three unidentified alleged drug pushers by Davao Death Squad members in or around 2013 in San Rafael, Davao City. Prosecutors said then-Davao City Mayor Rodrigo Duterte “instructed police DDS members that there was a job to be done against three alleged drug pushers.”
The filing also said P-0002’s statement appears to be the sole source for several allegations concerning Duterte’s conduct.

These include prosecution allegations that Duterte created a police “Death Squad”, told police DDS members they were being tasked as hitmen, ordered co-perpetrator Vicente Danao “to kill three or four men”, gave financial rewards to DDS handlers, and financed weapons and ammunition through this intelligence fund.
These allegations were raised in the prosecution’s case and were not established as findings by Trial Chamber III.

Aside from this, Haynes pointed to another redacted individual or entity that he referred to as the “sole source”, which has “not provided a sworn statement” about the circumstances of P-0002 and his situation, which remains concealed.
Much of Haynes’ allegation over that “sole source” is redacted, but he cited obscure statements that he said “reveal an intention to steer the proceedings”.
“Taken together, these shortcomings undermine P-0002’s descriptions of Mr. Duterte’s alleged actions,” Haynes argued.
“Given the Prosecution’s submission that P-0002 is [REDACTED] and in the absence of any supporting documentation, the only appropriate remedy is the exclusion of his evidence.”
Corroborations in P-0002’s evidence
Among the 62,000 items of evidence prosecutors disclosed to the defense, Haynes said they found no material corroborating claims about P-0002.
The defense also said the former policeman’s statement and associate materials “portray a witness deeply hostile towards Mr. Duterte and paint a picture of an individual who is emotionally unstable.”
Describing the materials, including handwritten notes whose contents are redacted, Haynes said P-0002’s evidence “reveals a paranoia” and “leads him to exaggerate” information.
“This aligns with P-0002’s erratic conduct,” Haynes argued.

The other batches of associated material, including two handwritten notes, an unsigned and undated typed affidavit, and a Philippine National Police personal data sheet, “were not used or commented on P-0002” and had no verification or authentication.
The defense also questioned how the interview was conducted, stating that a counsel appointed by Pre-Trial Chamber I at the time represented the defense “as an observer."

Calling it a “significant error”, Haynes said the previous counsel’s involvement was “negligible” and that their presence “was a formality” that gave “no substantive protection to a future defendant’s rights”.
Criminal records of witnesses, victims sought

In a separate filing, Duterte’s lawyers asked judges to order prosecutors to seek and disclose criminal history information concerning witnesses and victims identified in the prosecution’s updated Trial Brief.
The defense wants records of arrests, convictions, sentences, non-judicial dispositions, arrest warrants and Interpol notices.
It argued that such information may be relevant to witness credibility and may also be “potentially exculpatory.”
The defense singled out P-1302, whom it identified as the first prosecution witness expected to testify.
It said open-source material indicates that P-1302 has been the subject of a redacted number of legal cases in the Philippines, but no corresponding judicial records have been disclosed.
Duterte’s lawyers also said the criminal records of alleged victims could be relevant to testing the prosecution’s case theory on police claims of self-defense.

They argued that records showing an alleged victim had an arrest warrant or faced proceedings for an offense such as illegal possession of firearms could support the legitimacy of a particular police operation.
The defense asked the Chamber to order the prosecution to immediately seek and obtain requested information.
For witnesses expected to testify before January 1, 2027, it asked that the materials be disclosed no later than November 30.
Trial Chamber III has yet to rule on either request.
Duterte’s crimes against humanity trial is scheduled to open on November 30. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 45: Cale88 seen as small-time despite millions in money flows
articles.summary: The 45th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte began with the Senate impeachment court ordering OVP spokesperson Paolo Panelo to explain his remarks alleging bias by some…

blocks.text: The 45th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte began with the Senate impeachment court ordering OVP spokesperson Paolo Panelo to explain his remarks alleging bias by some senator-judges.
Panelo defended his comments as part of his freedom of speech.

Defense witness and Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo testified that Cale88 Foods Corp., a listed business interest of the Vice President’s husband, Manases Carpio, is a registered micro, small and medium enterprise.
Likewise, Rodolfo said the firm stopped operations in 2025 due to a change in ownership.
Rodolfo also said that, from 201 employees in 2024, the firm only had 50 workers in 2025 based on its submissions to the Board of Investments under DTI.

At the same time, Rodolfo testified that Cale88 only had zero and two employees in 2024 and 2025, respectively, based on the firm’s General Information Sheet submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
The witness said there was no reason for Cale88 Foods Corporation to surpass its declared sales of P208 million in 2022 to 2025.

He made the testimony after senator-judges pointed out that the money inflow and outflow to Cale88 accounts reached P1.2 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions based on the records of the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said it was puzzling that Cale88 did not apply for incentives when it registered before the BOI, which regulates fiscal incentives for firms and considering the billions worth of bank transactions that it recorded under its account.
Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said it "sounds bananas" that Cale88 was able to produce 422,000 kilos of banana chips in 2025 with only two employees and three officials.

Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Director Pilar Marilyn Pagayunan, meanwhile, testified that Cale88 Foods Corp. was granted product registration documents, or the Certificate of Product Registration.
The FDA official, however, said she won’t be able to testify on the capacity of Cale88 to produce over 400,000 kilos of banana chips.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero asked the defense team if they bought a sample of the banana chips.
Defense counsel Justin Gular, however, said the defense does not have samples of the chips.
Gular said they will present a proper witness who can speak on Cale88’s production.
The impeachment trial will resume on December 1 to give way to the ongoing Senate deliberations on the proposed P7.2 trillion budget for 2027.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: AFP eyes kinetic weapons to boost territorial defense
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) is eyeing the acquisition of kinetic weapon systems to strengthen the country's territorial defense and protect its sea lanes.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 11:28pm
The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) is eyeing the acquisition of kinetic weapon systems to strengthen the country's territorial defense and protect its sea lanes.

In a report by Chino Gaston on "24 Oras" on Friday, US President Donald Trump announced a $2-billion military loan for the Philippines during his visit to the country, equivalent to around P127 billion.
Of this amount, $400 million will be allocated to strengthening the military's capabilities to deter potential attacks in the West Philippine Sea.
One of the capabilities being considered involves kinetic weapons, which can strike targets at long range on land or at sea.
These weapons use the kinetic energy generated by the speed and mass of a projectile, such as missiles and bullets, to hit their targets.

"These are weapon systems which have larger range. So, there are missile systems. The missile systems will not be effective if there is no radar. Of course, you need to detect where the threat is," Major General Oliver Maquiling, director of the AFP's DAGITPA Exercise, said in a mix of English and Filipino.
AFP Chief of Staff General Antonio Nafarrete said these weapons are important in deterring foreign vessels from entering the country's sea lanes.

"We concentrate now on kinetic requirements basically for territorial defense talaga, ensuring pag may mga… kasi ito archipelagic. Pumapasok na yung mga PLA (People's Liberation Army) na mga naval vessels dito sa sea lines of communication natin. That’s international kasi, so we must have that deterrent capability," Nafarette said.

(We are now focusing on kinetic requirements, primarily for territorial defense. Given that the Philippines is an archipelagic country and Chinese naval vessels are entering our sea lines of communication, we must have that deterrent capability.)
The deployment and use of missile systems are among the capabilities being tested and practiced during the AFP's AJEX DAGITPA military exercises.
The Philippines already operates several missile systems, including the BrahMos cruise missiles acquired from India, which have a reported range of up to 300 kilometers.
The country also has C-Star anti-ship cruise missiles from South Korea. —Jean Mangaluz/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience
articles.summary: The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years…

image.caption: Brazil distributed more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and maintained its measles-free status; in the US, vaccination rates have fallenImage: ZUMA Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.
Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.
But it doesn't have to stay this way.

Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.
In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.
Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.
What Brazil does differently from the US
Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected case. Brazil's own rule is a ladder:

items: Report cases within 24 hours
Investigate within 48 hours
Vaccinate people close to the case within 72 hours

blocks.text: It has also made hunting for cases a national habit.
In a program called "Dia S", health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers, and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.
Brazil holds targeted, mass vaccination days called "Dia D". There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.
If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and they vaccinate them and other people living nearby.
The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of measles vaccination in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious; a country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.
"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.
Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis?
Why the US lost its measle-free status

The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

In August 2026, when US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children, it came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. As PAHO's Jarbas Barbosa says above, avoiding vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear; Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners unprotected.
In the Texas counties, where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved. In 24 states, so many children were exempt that those states couldn't reach the 95% threshold even if every other child got vaccinated.

But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 95% measles vaccination rule explained
It all comes down to math.

A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.
To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak start is likely to start.
In the US, where vaccination rates at kindergartens have dropped to 92%, that small difference is big enough to cause a measles outbreak.
The picture is mixed worldwide
Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.
But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.
Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.
Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.
Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.
But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as this time (November) in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.
What you need to know about measles
Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.
But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

articles.title: Germany face belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag
articles.summary: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.

image.caption: Based on their FIFA rankings, the Germany-Belgium matchup should produce a closely contested tieImage: Peter Schatz/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals—after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.
"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.

"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."
Historical success for Germany against Belgium
The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.
Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.
Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway – a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.
In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.
The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

articles.title: Marcos rejects call to reassess economic team amid 'malaise'
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday stood by his current economic team even as he was urged by a senator to take a closer look at his Cabinet amid a so-called “economic malaise.”

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 10:44pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday stood by his current economic team even as he was urged by a senator to take a closer look at his Cabinet amid a so-called “economic malaise.”

In a Kapihan with the media in Shenzhen, China, the President said he disagrees with the call of Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who earlier raised concerns about the dipping Philippine stocks, the weakening peso, and rising inflation, among other issues.
“No, I don’t…I disagree with him. I’m sorry, but I disagree with him,” Marcos said.
“All the difficulties we’re going under can be clearly directly traced to the war in Iran,” he added.
Cabinet revamp
Marcos likewise addressed speculations about recent changes in his Cabinet, saying that he is only trying to “put the best people to the best use” amid developments worldwide.
“Everything was done for a particular reason. There’s no general reason that I’m not happy with the Cabinet or anything like that. No, not at all. Quite the contrary,” he said.
“Issues come up that didn’t exist before in certain departments. So we’re trying to put the people who are best able to address those issues into the proper department,” he added.
The President said that the reshuffle also had something to do with his administration’s plans.
“[We’re] trying to get the best people into whatever position we need to best be able to push our priorities for the future,” he said.
Marcos also stood firm that shifting one Cabinet member to another position does not produce instability in the government.

“The job of a Cabinet secretary does not remain exactly the same from day one until day whatever it is six years later. Nagbabago talaga ‘yan (it really changes). And then we make our own plans as we go along,” he said.

“And then we have to worry about shocks like the war in Iran, so we have to adjust also to that. And then now with AI coming up, we have to adjust also to that. And then the different developments in geopolitics, we also have to adjust to that,” he added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Martin Romualdez's co-accused surrenders, granted conditional immunity
articles.summary: A co-accused of Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co in the plunder charges they are facing before the Sandiganbayan surrendered on Friday to the National Bureau of…

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 8:53pm

A co-accused of Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez and former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co in the plunder charges they are facing before the Sandiganbayan surrendered on Friday to the National Bureau of Investigation.

According to the Office of the Ombudsman Felicito Guevarra, the president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., was granted conditional immunity "because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case."

"Samchan has returned to the Bureau of the Treasury all its earnings from the questioned transactions. Restitution does not erase criminal liability. It is also not the basis of the immunity," the Ombudsman said in a statement.

"The Office granted Mr. Guevarra conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 because his testimony and records are necessary to establish the truth in this case. The immunity rests on his full and truthful testimony," it added.
The Ombudsman said the conditions are as follows:

items: that Guevarra will cooperate fully and truthfully turn over all of Samchan's records and devices;
that he will remain in the country; and
that he will stay under DOJ protection.

blocks.text: "If he breaks any condition, his immunity will be revoked and his prosecution will resume," the Ombudsman said.
Guevarra personally handled Samchan's operations, said the Ombudsman.
"His testimony and records will help the prosecution trace the movement of funds alleged in the charge sheet. The charges against the other accused stand as filed," the Ombudsman said.
"All accused are presumed innocent. The evidence will be presented in court," it added. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
articles.summary:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that

blocks.text: The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Rohingya refugees attend a rally addressed by the UN general assembly president, Khalilur Rahman, in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh on Friday. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters

blocks.text: “The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the Rohingya refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. Photograph: Salahuddin Ahmed/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Perez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

The text message that came from inside the…

blocks.text: The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

blocks.caption: The Port Isabel detention center in Los Fresnos, Texas. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

blocks.caption: Children look at posters honoring Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, shot dead by federal agents in Minneapolis in January. Photograph: Tim Evans/Reuters

blocks.text: Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

blocks.caption: An examination area of the Port Isabel facility. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

blocks.caption: A security guard at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

blocks.caption: The barbed-wire fence at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/Reuters

blocks.text: Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

articles.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
articles.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But…

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has halted all further investments in German manufacturing for the time being and is also weighing plant closuresImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
Can crisis reinvent the car again?
German auto industry faces restructuring

Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.

"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."

A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.

blocks.caption: In Germany, Mercedes has three assembly plants and seven facilities that manufacture drivetrains and componentsImage: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

blocks.text: Unions dig in amid fight for survival

Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.

blocks.caption: Mercedes plans more than 40 model launches by next year — a growing share will be built outside GermanyImage: Joan Cros/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'

A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.

These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.

Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.

Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.

In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.

As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

articles.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
articles.summary: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down

blocks.text: Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.

Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
after newsletter promotion
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

articles.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.summary:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that

blocks.text: California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
after newsletter promotion
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

articles.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
articles.summary:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive…

blocks.text: Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California.
